concept.name: Put-call parity
concept.definition: Put-call parity is a no-arbitrage identity linking the prices of a European call and a European put at the same strike and expiration to the underlying's forward price: a long call plus a short put replicates a forward contract, so their price difference must equal the discounted difference between the forward price and the strike.
concept.intuition: Whether the stock finishes above or below the strike, one of the two options is exercised and you end up buying at the strike — exactly like a forward — so the two packages must cost the same today.
concept.mechanics: Formally C - P = D x (F - K), or in spot terms C - P = S - PV(K) for non-dividend stocks, extended to C - P = S - PV(K) - PV(dividends) when dividends are paid. The identity is model-free (static replication) and underlies synthetic positions, conversions/reversals, and the equivalence of covered calls to cash-secured puts; violations beyond transaction costs imply arbitrage.
concept.formula: C - P = S_0 - K*e^(-rT) - PV(dividends); equivalently C + PV(K) = P + S_0 (fiduciary call = married put).
concept.failure_modes: Parity holds exactly only for European options in frictionless markets; American early-exercise rights, dividends, borrow costs, and wide bid-ask spreads create bands within which deviations persist without being exploitable. During market stress, financing and borrow constraints widen these bands dramatically.
concept.misconceptions: Parity is not a pricing model that predicts option values — it is a consistency condition among prices that already exist. Nor does it require assumptions about volatility or the underlying's distribution.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, one-year $100-strike European call at $8.00, and the risk-free rate near zero, parity implies the $100 put should trade near $8.00 too; if it traded at $5.00, a conversion would lock in the $3.00 discrepancy.
